**Remark.** The statement calls $f \wedge g$ the "pointwise maximum", but the defining formula is $\map {\paren {f \wedge g} } s = \min \set {\map f s, \map g s}$; this is just a wording slip (it is the pointwise minimum). We prove the claim for the mapping as defined by that formula.

**Proof.** Both $f \wedge g$ and $h := \dfrac 1 2 \paren {f + g - \size {f - g} }$ are mappings $S \to \R$. By the definitions of pointwise addition, pointwise difference, absolute value of a real-valued function and pointwise scalar multiplication, for every $s \in S$:
$$\map h s = \frac 1 2 \paren {\map f s + \map g s - \size {\map f s - \map g s} }.$$
Two mappings with the same domain and codomain are equal iff they agree at every point, so it suffices to show $\map h s = \min \set {\map f s, \map g s}$ for each $s \in S$.

Fix $s \in S$ and write $a = \map f s$, $b = \map g s$, real numbers. By trichotomy/totality of the order on $\R$, either $a \le b$ or $b < a$.

*Case $a \le b$.* Then $a - b \le 0$, so $\size {a - b} = -\paren {a - b} = b - a$, and $\min \set {a, b} = a$. Hence
$$\frac 1 2 \paren {a + b - \size {a - b} } = \frac 1 2 \paren {a + b - b + a} = \frac 1 2 \cdot 2a = a = \min \set {a, b}.$$

*Case $b < a$.* Then $a - b > 0$, so $\size {a - b} = a - b$, and $\min \set {a, b} = b$. Hence
$$\frac 1 2 \paren {a + b - \size {a - b} } = \frac 1 2 \paren {a + b - a + b} = \frac 1 2 \cdot 2b = b = \min \set {a, b}.$$

In both cases $\map h s = \min \set {\map f s, \map g s} = \map {\paren {f \wedge g} } s$. As $s \in S$ was arbitrary, $f \wedge g = \dfrac 1 2 \paren {f + g - \size {f - g} }$. (If $S = \varnothing$ both sides are the empty mapping and the equality holds trivially; the argument above covers this vacuously.) $\blacksquare$
